enrichment.short_title: Special reasons defence where motor insurance lapsed by non-payment
key_facts: Mrs Smith pleaded guilty to using a motor vehicle without insurance after her insurer cancelled cover when direct debit premium payments failed.
She received no notification of cancellation because a recorded-delivery letter did not arrive.
The justices rejected her argument that ignorance of the lapse constituted special reasons not to endorse her licence with six penalty points.
On appeal by case stated, the Divisional Court held the justices had not misdirected themselves in distinguishing mistaken belief from active misleading.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' endorsement decision following conviction for driving without insurance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the justices' refusal to find special reasons was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: An honest but mistaken belief that insurance was in force does not amount to special reasons unless it is based on reasonable grounds or the defendant was actively misled; a motorist who fails to maintain premium payments remains responsible for ensuring cover is in force, and failure of postal notification does not excuse that duty.
legal_issues: Meaning of special reasons under section 44 of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988
Whether justices required proof of active misleading rather than honest mistaken belief
Application of insurance special-reasons authorities to lapsed direct-debit cover

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of cold water test for vibration white finger benefits

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: NACODS challenged the Secretary of State's refusal to amend Notes on the Diagnosis of Prescribed Diseases concerning the cold water provocation test for prescribed disease A11 (vibration white finger).
South Wales miners' benefit appeals showed medical advisers frequently used a negative CWPT result in ways inconsistent with departmental policy.
Expert evidence indicated the simple immersion test produced unreliable false positives and negatives and was of negligible diagnostic value.
The Secretary of State accepted a positive result might assist claimants but maintained a negative result should not support refusal of benefit, yet did not state this in the NDPD.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim challenging the Secretary of State's decision not immediately to revise non-statutory diagnostic guidance for industrial injuries benefit.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; the Secretary of State was ordered to modify guidance so a negative cold water provocation test is treated as of no diagnostic value.
enrichment.ratio: Where departmental policy is that a negative cold water provocation test must not support an unfavourable PDA11 diagnosis but written guidance encourages use of the test, it is irrational to leave that policy unstated when evidence shows a significant risk that medical advisers treat negative results as diagnostically significant.
legal_issues: Wednesbury unreasonableness of maintaining NDPD cold water provocation guidance
Diagnostic criteria for prescribed disease A11
Whether negative CWPT results were being misapplied by Benefits Agency medical advisers
Scope of judicial review of non-statutory departmental medical guidance

enrichment.short_title: Nepalese Maoist asylum appeal remitted for inconsistent tribunal reasoning
key_facts: Mr Gurung, a low-level Nepalese Communist Party (Maoist) student leader, sought asylum after police issued a nationwide arrest warrant.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal found prosecution would be legitimate and that he faced no real risk of ill-treatment in detention.
Five days later, in Indra Gurung, a differently constituted tribunal made broadly contrary findings about risks faced by Maoists in Nepal.
The Court of Appeal held the tribunal in Shyam Gurung's case had not adequately reasoned its conclusions in light of the conflicting authority.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from an Immigration Appeal Tribunal determination refusing asylum.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the matter was remitted to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal for rehearing, with directions for the President to consider constitution and conduct.
enrichment.ratio: Even where Article 1F is not engaged and separate tribunal decisions bind only on their facts, an asylum tribunal must reason fully where its conclusions on country risk appear irreconcilable with very recent broadly stated findings of another tribunal division on the same country conditions.
legal_issues: Risk of persecution versus legitimate prosecution of Maoist activists
Treatment of detainees with Maoist connections in Nepal
Effect of inconsistent IAT country guidance decisions
Whether Article 1F exclusion was applied

enrichment.short_title: Health and safety inspector power to require written answers

statutes_considered.title: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974

key_facts: Wandsworth laid an information against Travis Perkins' health and safety manager for failing to answer an inspector's questions about forklift training.
The inspector had sought information by letter from Northamptonshire after routine inspections raised competence concerns.
A district judge held section 20(2)(j) permitted only face-to-face questioning and dismissed the prosecution.
The Divisional Court held written questions and answers were permitted where necessary for investigation across a local authority's limited geographical jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review challenge to a district judge's ruling on the construction of section 20(2)(j), proceeding by direct challenge rather than case stated.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed; the district judge's order was quashed and the summons was remitted to a different tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: Section 20(2)(j) of the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 should be construed broadly to permit inspectors to obtain relevant information in writing as well as face to face, since the power is for investigation only, inspectors lack entry powers outside their authority area, and nothing in the subsection excludes written exchange.
legal_issues: Construction of section 20(2)(j) Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
Whether health and safety inspectors may require answers in writing
Effect of the sweeping-up power in section 20(2)(m)
Practical limits on local authority enforcement investigations

enrichment.short_title: Crown Court wrongly allowed appeal for absent prosecution counsel
key_facts: Richard Proud appealed convictions for common assault and threatening behaviour to Portsmouth Crown Court.
CPS counsel was briefed in two courts listed at 10.30 and was prosecuting in another court when Judge Hughes called on Proud's appeal.
The judge allowed the appeal because no prosecutor was present, depriving victims of compensation awards.
Counsel arrived within minutes but the appeal had already been allowed and could not be reinstated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Crown Court's decision to allow a defendant's appeal in the absence of prosecution counsel.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed; the appeal was remitted to a differently constituted court for determination.
enrichment.ratio: A Crown Court judge acts unlawfully in allowing an appeal solely because prosecution counsel is briefly absent without balancing the interests of the appellant, victims and the public interest, making enquiries as to when counsel will arrive, or considering less punitive alternatives such as adjournment or costs sanctions.
legal_issues: Wednesbury reasonableness of allowing an appeal for non-appearance of prosecution
Duties of counsel under the Bar Code of Conduct when accepting clashing briefs

enrichment.short_title: Security for costs refused against Monaco resident claimant
key_facts: Mr Somerset-Leeke, resident in Monaco for tax purposes, and trustee company Brunel Trustees Ltd pursued a Chancery claim.
Defendants sought security for costs on grounds including out-of-jurisdiction residence and asset movement.
The application was procedurally muddled and did not clearly identify which CPR grounds were relied upon.
Jacob J held English judgments could be registered and enforced in Monaco without requiring disclosure of assets abroad.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a master's refusal to order security for costs under CPR 25.13.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no order for security for costs against either claimant.
enrichment.ratio: Residence outside the Brussels/Lugano Convention area does not justify security for costs unless enforcement risk justifies it; a claimant cannot be required to disclose asset location as a condition of resisting security under ground (a), and moving abroad before litigation without evidence of evasive intent does not engage ground (g).
legal_issues: Exercise of discretion under CPR 25.13 for out-of-jurisdiction claimants
Enforceability of English costs orders in Monaco
Security against a claimant company acting as pension trustee
Whether relocation to Monaco constituted steps to evade enforcement

enrichment.short_title: Murder conviction appeal on witness credibility and fresh psychiatric evidence
key_facts: Terence Smith was convicted of murder with co-defendant Harry Groves for killing Simon Shannon in Clacton-on-Sea in May 1995.
Prosecution relied heavily on confessions reported by Paul Courtman and Steven Sparkes; the appellant denied involvement.
Prosecution did not call Adam Crossland, whose later statements undermined his earlier account; the defence chose not to call him either.
On appeal, fresh psychiatric evidence about Groves was held immaterial to Smith's involvement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction for murder following trial at Norwich Crown Court in October 1997.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the conviction was held safe.
enrichment.ratio: A prosecutor may properly decline to call a witness of primary facts who is not credible without making the conviction unsafe; fresh evidence casting doubt on a co-defendant's reliability does not undermine conviction where pathological and confession evidence still supports the appellant's participation.

Impact of not calling Adam Crossland on fairness of trial
Admissibility and materiality of fresh psychiatric evidence about co-defendant Groves

enrichment.short_title: Port equipment damages measured by Saudi market value not European resale price
key_facts: A container of gas lighters exploded at Damman port, destroying the claimants' straddle carrier and dock truck beyond repair.
Carriers were held liable under Saudi port rules imposing strict liability on terminal users.
The judge awarded US$115,800 based on European second-hand equipment prices; the claimants sought US$200,000 and US$26,600 respectively.
Expert evidence showed Saudi market value reflected transport, import, tropicalisation and related costs not captured by European resale figures.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court quantum award after liability was established at trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; damages increased to US$227,400 plus agreed trailer repair costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where tortious destruction of chattels is governed by English law, the claimant recovers market or resale value at the time and place of loss; value in Saudi Arabia must reflect the costs of importing and adapting equipment for use there, not merely the price of buying second-hand equipment in Europe.
legal_issues: Measure of damages for destruction of port handling equipment
Market value versus replacement cost
Assessment of value where there is no local second-hand market
Application of The Maersk Colombo principles
